At the bottom of the vellum parchment was pressed an authentic wax seal featuring a two-headed imperial eagle, proving beyond doubt that the text had once belonged to the private library of the Mustansiriya Madrasah.

text: Deep beneath the stone shadow of Kirkuk's ancient Citadel stood the subterranean bakery of the Burhan family, where glowing wood embers had fired vaulted clay ovens continuously since the end of the First World War.
Seventeen-year-old Basil woke at three every morning, hauling sacks of coarse stone-ground whole wheat down the narrow stairs into the flour-dusted workspace.

The true soul of the bakery was not its antique brick arches, but a heavy earthenware crock kept wrapped in burlap inside a temperature-controlled wooden pantry. Inside lived a fermented sourdough starter culture that Master Burhan's grandfather had first kneaded in 1918.
Every loaf of dark, crusty flatbread derived its tangy aroma, golden crust, and airy crumb structure from daily feedings of spring water and fresh flour mixed with this living heritage.

One stormy evening, faulty electrical wiring in the adjacent storage room sparked an aggressive fire. While others panicked and fled to the street, Basil remembered the fragile crock; he soaked an apron in water, wrapped his face, and retrieved the earthenware mother safely before smoke consumed the hall.

When the bakery was rebuilt with modern fire-suppression equipment, Master Burhan named Basil his junior partner. At the grand reopening, the aroma of sourdough was proof that ancestral spirit endures when protected with courage.
